title: I want to build an AI-assisted city-building game like Cities: Skylines, SimCity, or Tropico. Where should I start?
author: Mysterious_Pin_1244
selftext:
Hey everyone!

I'm looking for some advice from people who have experience developing games with AI assistance.

My goal is to create a **city-building and management simulation game**, inspired by games like:

* **SimCity (2013)** – City planning, infrastructure, utilities, and simulation.
* **Cities: Skylines** – Road networks, zoning, traffic, population, and economic systems.
* **Tropico series** – Politics, citizens, resource management, economy, and decision-making.

I'm particularly interested in building a game with interconnected systems: population growth, individual citizen needs, employment, housing, transportation, public services, economy, and city development.

I know this is a very ambitious project, especially for a solo developer, and I'm not expecting AI to magically build an entire game for me. I'm willing to start small, learn along the way, and gradually expand the project.

However, I'd really like to **leverage AI as much as possible throughout the development process**, from planning and architecture to programming, debugging, asset creation, and testing.

**I'd love to hear your recommendations on a few things:**

**1. Game engine and technology stack**

* Would you recommend Unity, Unreal Engine 5, Godot, or something else for this type of simulation?
* Which engine works best with AI coding assistants?
* What technologies or programming languages would you choose for complex simulation systems?

**2. AI tools and coding assistants**

* What AI tools are you currently using for game development?
* Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, local LLMs, or something else?
* Have you successfully used AI agents to develop larger game systems?
* Are there any useful GitHub projects, frameworks, or agent-based workflows worth exploring?

**3. Prompt engineering and project organization**

* How would you structure prompts for a project of this scale?
* Is it better to use detailed design documents, specifications, and small development tasks?
* How do you maintain consistency across a large AI-assisted codebase?
* Do you use files like AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or custom instructions to guide your AI agents?
* Any examples of effective prompts or workflows would be incredibly helpful!

**4. Simulation architecture**

* How would you approach simulating thousands of citizens, buildings, jobs, and economic interactions?
* Would you use individual agents, aggregated population models, ECS, or a hybrid approach?
* How would you design systems that interact without becoming impossible to maintain?

**5. Where should I actually begin?**

* What would be a realistic first playable prototype?
* Which systems should I prioritize?
* What common mistakes should I avoid when developing a management game with AI assistance?

**My long-term vision** is to build a living, evolving city where player decisions have meaningful consequences, with interconnected economic, social, and infrastructure systems.

I'm not trying to recreate Cities: Skylines overnight. I want to establish a solid technical foundation and build something progressively.

I'm especially interested in hearing from anyone who has attempted a similar project using AI, whether successful or not.

**If you were starting a city-building game today with AI as your main development assistant, what engine, tools, models, and workflow would you choose, and why?**

Any advice, resources, GitHub repositories, prompting examples, or lessons learned would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks in advance!

comments.author: No-Pollution7797
comments.body:
I'd start with the simulation and no graphics at all. A small grid, three or four numbers per cell like housing, jobs and land value, and one function that advances a day and prints the result is small enough for an AI assistant to write and for you to actually read.



For thousands of citizens I'd go aggregated first, counts per block instead of individual people, and only simulate individuals for whatever the player looks at up close. I work on a text game with a lot of saved state, and the habit I'd build early with AI-written code is tests for the rules, since an assistant will happily change a formula in one place and break a system three files away.

comments.author: crackedpotstudio
comments.body:
Interesting topic and good luck with your project!

I'm currently working on an bonsai farming rpg (check out my profile if you would like to see more) but I've had some fun with some sideprojects building an grand strategy meets rts meets city builder.

To answer your questions from my own perspective:

Engine, combining claude code with Godot 4 really makes things so easy nowadays. Create a godot project, create a new environment in claude code and point it to your godot project folder and you're ready to go.

AI Tools, claude code with Pixellab and Tripo3d integrated. I have 3 custom agents, 1 for creating pixelart through pixellab, 1 for making animations and 1 for debugging/stresstesting and backwards savegame compatibility checker.

Prompt engineering, not really that much concerned with it anymore since the latest models are becoming increasingly better. But I have a claude project dedicated to my game which I sometimes use to help me set up initial prompts, rules and agents.

Simulation, I would just start discussing with your claude project on how to tackle this.

Where to begin, start a godot project and a claude code worktree and just start trying stuff.

comments.author: Aggravating-Vehicle9
comments.body:
Hey, happy to talk about this. I think your first challenge will be to figure out the architecture - pretty much everything will be downstream of that. 

Games get interesting when simple gameplay elements become composable in interesting and unexpected ways. That's the essence of a good game - like chess where a set of simple move-sets can result in huge variety. 

The questions you will need to ponder 

What gameplay systems exist to support your core "loop" 

What are the minimum set of composable features that can build those systems? 

What architecture supports all of those components? 

Anyway... hmu on chat if you want to talk about this sort of thing.

comments.author: egonosz
comments.body:
I would start with that:

why do you want to build this game?  
Do you want it to build, just for your sake or do you want to sell it?

If for your sake just do whatever. If you actually want to sell it, ask yourself why anyone would want to play your game and not the other games in the same genre.

If you answered the question about what your game would do differently or more interestingly, first prototype that idea. Look at it how it feels and if it would actually sell your game. (If it is possible to prototype.)

I want to mention the prototyping is important, because for most people to find out if an idea would actually work in a game without trying it, is extremely hard. Many times studios skip features only, because they tried it and it didn’t work.

comments.author: Meatt
comments.body:
I use Deepseek Harness with Godot MCP, and pay for v4.1 Flash. It's cheap and really decent at coding what I tell it, I haven't had to manually edit code at all. It can create placeholder art but nothing high quality, that will have to come from you or another LLM that's good at it. It's great art implementing the supplied art though.

Or pay for Claude Opus 5.5 and use Godot MCP, sounds like Opus is incredible so far, I just haven't needed to switch yet.

Deepseek Harness will even help edit your config files to set up the mcp's if you ask it.

Just come up with your own design for the game, think about what could be clever and different about YOUR vision, and start implementing small slices at a time and expand. Good luck!

comments.author: jawni
comments.body:
IMO you should be asking the AI these questions, and not because you'll get bad answers here, you generally won't, but because you won't be able to iterate back and forth on the idea as quickly and a lot of these questions are interdependent which means answering them all and having each answer reconcile with each other is important.

I would suggest starting on the project and then coming back with more specific implementation questions.

I think you'll find a game like this is actually deceptively simple in some ways and deceptively complex in others.

comments.author: ledniv
comments.body:
Personally, I would keep the simulation as separate **data** and **logic**. Citizens can just be integer indices into arrays containing things like position, home, job, money, hunger, happiness, etc. Then write logic that processes those arrays. The GameObjects or whatever engine you use should mostly be there to show the results.

There is another big benefit to doing it this way: you can run the simulation without rendering anything. That makes it much easier to test whether your economy actually works, simulate days or years very quickly, and find problems before you even have all the visuals.

Since you are planning to use AI heavily, I would also give the agent architectural rules before it starts writing lots of code. Otherwise it is very easy to end up with thousands of little objects, components, events, and relationships that become increasingly difficult for both you and the AI to understand.

I made a free Data Oriented Design skill for coding agents that does exactly that:

[https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design](https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design)

Small plug: I also wrote *High Performance Unity Game Development with Data Oriented Design*. Despite Unity being in the title, a lot of the architecture is engine agnostic, and simulation heavy games like city builders are exactly where these ideas become really useful.

[https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development](https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development)
